script.opening: (Hesitant, quiet, long pauses, avoids looking at the camera.) "This is hard to talk about … sex has become really painful, and sometimes I just … freeze, or everything tightens up and I can't. It's affecting my relationship. I think it might be connected to … something that happened to me years ago. I've never really told anyone. Can you fix it?"

facts.text: "It's when we try. Everything just clamps shut." Pain at the entrance on attempted penetration; has not been able to use tampons for years. About a year with her current partner, worse in the last 6 months. Fine with non-penetrative intimacy.

"I'm not sure. I haven't really paid attention to that" — no unusual discharge, itching, sores or white patches she knows of; no bleeding after sex or between periods; periods regular, not especially painful. Cervical screening up to date (had to stop once).
Will say only, if asked gently: assaulted by an ex-partner when she was 19. Won't give details unless she chooses. "Sometimes it just comes back, when things get close." Never reported it.
"No. I'm safe now. It was years ago." Current partner, Sam, is kind and patient; no abuse.
"No, not that. Just stressed and down about it." Occasional nightmares. No thoughts of self-harm. Drinks a little at weekends.
No medicines apart from the combined pill. No allergies. Works as a primary school administrator.
"That it's because of what happened. That I'm broken somehow." "That it won't get better, and it'll wreck my relationship. And that I'll have to talk about it all in detail." Dreading being examined.

Fragile; ready to withdraw if pushed. If the doctor says examination is her choice and not needed today: "(Relieved.) That helps. I was dreading that." If the doctor pushes for an examination or details, go quiet and say "Maybe I should go." Comforted by hearing it's common and treatable: "Really? I thought it was just me." Happy to do self-swabs. Doesn't want police: "I don't want to go to the police. But the support sounds good."

ice.ideas: "It's because of what happened to me — I'm broken somehow."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — first disclosure of a past assault; fear of judgement, of having to tell it all, of an examination; fear of losing her relationship.

cues: "Something that happened to me years ago." — receive gently, don't push.
"I've never really told anyone." — acknowledge her courage.
"Everything tightens up." — involuntary response, not her fault.

checkpoints.text: Receives the disclosure with BELIEF and validation, thanks her for her trust, and does not press for details she isn’t ready to share — letting her lead

Goes at HER PACE and explicitly does NOT force/rush an intimate examination — makes any examination her choice, deferrable, consent-led with control and a chaperone (GMC 2024), arranged face to face as it cannot be done on video, and only if clinically necessary (often none at the first visit)
Recognises and VALIDATES the likely trauma link (freezing/involuntary tightening — vaginismus/trauma response with dyspareunia) as a real, understandable response, not a failing
Keeps organic/contributing causes in mind (infection, lichen sclerosus, atrophy, endometriosis) to be assessed sensitively over time — without overriding the trauma-informed pace

Offers the right support and referrals (psychosexual therapy, trauma-focused psychology/counselling, specialist/sexual-assault support), screens current SAFETY (NICE PH50) and MOOD/PTSD (NICE NG116), makes clear that reporting to the police is her choice as an adult, and gives realistic HOPE about treatment
Hands her CONTROL throughout, makes her feel safe and believed, and avoids judgement or pressure
Holds the disclosure with compassion and does not reduce her to a physical problem nor push examination

Safety-nets and follows up: a paced supportive plan, support/referral information to take in her own time, safety/mood follow-up, and an open door — trauma-informed care that treats both trauma and sexual difficulty

worked.txt: "Thank you for telling me — I know that can’t have been easy, especially if you’ve not told anyone before. I believe you, and I’m really glad you’ve come. We’ll go entirely at your pace today."

"I want to be clear about one thing up front: I am NOT going to examine you unless and until YOU want me to — that could only ever happen face to face, with a chaperone if you’d like one. There’s no rush, no pressure — we can talk and make a plan, and any examination is completely your choice, with you in control, whenever you’re ready, if at all."

"What you describe — freezing, everything tightening — is a very real and understandable way your body protects itself after what happened. It’s not you failing or anything being ‘wrong’ with you. And importantly, it’s treatable."
"At some point, when you’re comfortable, it can help to check there’s nothing physical adding to the pain — but only when you’re ready, and only if you want to. There’s no hurry."

"There’s genuinely effective help — specialist psychosexual therapy for the physical side, and trauma-focused counselling for what happened. Many people get much better. I can also share details of services that support people after assault, for whenever you want them. And whether you ever tell the police is completely your decision — now, later or never."

"Can I gently check — are you safe now, no one currently hurting you? … Good. There’s no timetable here. Take what you need, come back when you’re ready, and we’ll keep going together. You’re in charge of this."

f.learning: Sexual difficulty disclosed alongside a past sexual assault calls for trauma-informed care, and the way the disclosure is received shapes everything: respond with belief, validation and gratitude for her trust, without pressing for details she is not ready to share, and let her lead how much she says. The central principle is to go at HER pace and explicitly NOT force or rush an intimate examination — a forced or hurried exam would retraumatise her — so make clear that any examination is entirely her choice, can wait, and would only happen when she feels ready, with consent, control (she can stop at any time), a chaperone and explanation (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024), face to face rather than on video, and only if clinically necessary; often the first consultation involves no examination at all, with trust and a plan coming first. Recognise and validate the likely trauma link: "freezing" and involuntary tightening suggest a trauma/anxiety response and/or vaginismus (involuntary pelvic-floor spasm; genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder in DSM-5, international) with dyspareunia, a common and treatable consequence of sexual trauma, and it is a real, understandable protective response of body and mind, not a failing — a reframing that is itself therapeutic. Keep organic and contributing causes in mind (infection, lichen sclerosus, atrophy/dryness, endometriosis) to be assessed gently over time so nothing treatable is missed, without overriding the trauma-informed pace. Offer the right support — psychosexual therapy, trauma-focused psychological therapy/counselling, specialist and sexual-assault support services — with information she can take in her own time, screen current safety (NICE PH50) and mood/PTSD symptoms (NICE NG116: trauma-focused CBT, with EMDR as an option), make clear that as an adult she alone decides whether to report the assault to the police, and give realistic hope, as vaginismus and trauma responses have good treatment. The hidden agenda is hope mixed with shame, fear of judgement and the weight of a first disclosure; hand her control, make her feel safe and believed, avoid reducing her to a physical problem or pushing examination, and set a paced, supportive plan.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG116 (2018) · NICE PH50 (2014) · GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024) · GMC Confidentiality (2017) · DSM-5 genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (international)
knowledge.summary: Painful sex with freezing after a past sexual assault is usually a trauma and muscle-guarding response. Believe her, give her control, never push an examination, and keep physical causes in view.

points.t: Involuntary tightening of the pelvic floor on attempted penetration (vaginismus; genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder in DSM-5, international), often with pain and fear of pain. It is a recognised and treatable response to sexual trauma.

points.h: Physical causes to keep in view
points.t: Infection (thrush, STIs), vulval skin conditions such as lichen sclerosus, vaginal dryness, and deep pain from endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease. Many can be assessed by history and self-taken swabs before any examination.

GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain why an examination is needed and what it involves, offer a chaperone, get consent, and stop if she asks. Only examine if clinically necessary; after trauma it can be delayed until she is ready.

Ask about flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance and hypervigilance. NICE NG116: offer individual trauma-focused CBT for adults with PTSD or clinically important symptoms; EMDR is an option for non-combat trauma more than 3 months ago. Do not offer drug treatment to prevent PTSD.
NICE PH50: ask about domestic abuse in a private, safe setting. If there is current abuse, assess risk and refer to specialist domestic abuse services.

For an adult, whether to report to the police is her decision. Sexual assault referral centres (SARCs) and rape crisis services support people after both recent and past assaults. Confidentiality holds unless others, such as children, are at risk of serious harm (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

dg.d: Checked privacy; open question; let her disclose at her own pace; thanked her.
Explored the impact on her relationship, her stress and low mood, and her current safety.
No examination today; offered self-taken swabs; examination later only if needed, with consent, a chaperone and control.
Vaginismus or trauma response vs infection, lichen sclerosus, dryness, endometriosis or pelvic infection; superficial vs deep pain.
Screened for PTSD symptoms, suicidal thoughts and current abuse.
Explained the likely trauma-related tightening in plain words, with physical causes still to exclude.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Trauma-focused therapy and psychosexual referral; sexual-assault support services; police reporting left to her; shared decision on priorities.
Addressed mood, the relationship and possible physical contributors.
Review in a few weeks with swab results; mood and safety safety-net; open door.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’ve never really told anyone” and “can you fix it?” and responded to both.
Idea (it’s because of what happened; she is “broken”), concern (it won’t improve, having to recount it), expectation (to be fixed).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — first disclosure of a past assault; fear of judgement, of having to tell it all, of an examination; fear of losing her relationship — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Ms Forbes, I’m Dr Ahmed. Are you somewhere private where you can talk? Take your time — what would you like to talk about today?

This is hard to talk about. Sex has become really painful, and sometimes I just freeze, or everything tightens up and I can’t. It’s affecting my relationship. I think it might be connected to something that happened to me years ago. I’ve never really told anyone. Can you fix it?

Thank you for telling me. I know that can’t have been easy, especially if you’ve never told anyone. I believe you, and I’m really glad you’ve come. We’ll go entirely at your pace, and you don’t need to tell me anything you don’t want to.
model.why: Receives the disclosure with belief and without pressing for detail

model.text: Okay. Thank you.
I also want to say this now so you’re not worrying about it: I’m not going to ask you to have an examination today. If one is ever useful, it will be your choice, when you’re ready.
model.why: Removes the fear of a forced examination early

model.text: (Relieved.) That helps. I was dreading that.
Can you tell me more about the pain? Is it at the entrance when you first try, or deeper inside?
It’s when we try. Everything just clamps shut.
That tightening is something your body does on its own, a bit like flinching. Is there any itching, soreness, discharge, bleeding, or pain at other times, like with periods or passing urine?
model.why: Screens for infection, skin conditions and pelvic causes

model.text: I’m not sure. I haven’t really paid attention to that.
That’s fine. We can look into those gently later. When you think about what happened, or during sex, do you get memories that come back, nightmares, or feel on edge a lot of the time?
Sometimes it just comes back, when things get close.
And how has your mood been? Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Screens for mood and suicide risk

model.text: No, not that. Just stressed and down about it.
Thank you. I ask everyone this: is anyone hurting you now, or are you ever frightened of anyone at home?
model.why: Routine screen for current abuse (NICE PH50)

model.text: No. I’m safe now. It was years ago.
What do you think is going on, in your own mind?
That it’s because of what happened. That I’m broken somehow.
That’s a painful thought to carry. What worries you most about it?
That it won’t get better, and it’ll wreck my relationship. And that I’ll have to talk about it all in detail.

You’re not broken. What you describe — freezing and everything tightening — is your body trying to protect you after something frightening. It’s a real, recognised response, and it’s treatable. Many people get much better.
model.why: Validates the trauma link and gives hope

model.text: Really? I thought it was just me.

Really. It’s also sensible to check there’s nothing physical adding to the pain, like an infection or a skin problem. Some of that can be done with swabs you take yourself, in private. An examination could come later, only if needed and only if you want it, with a chaperone, and you could stop at any moment.
model.why: Keeps organic causes in view without overriding her pace

model.text: Swabs myself I could do.

There are two kinds of help. A psychosexual therapist works on the tightening and on getting back to a sex life that feels safe, often at your own pace step by step. And trauma-focused therapy helps with the memories that come back. Which feels most important to you?
model.why: Offers psychosexual and trauma-focused therapy and shares the decision

model.text: Probably both. But the memories first.

Then I’ll refer you for trauma-focused talking therapy, and to psychosexual services. You don’t have to report anything to the police unless you want to — that’s your choice, now or in the future. I can also give you details of services that support people after sexual assault, to use whenever you’re ready.
model.why: Respects her choice on reporting and signposts support

model.text: I don’t want to go to the police. But the support sounds good.
That’s completely your decision. Would it help to have some information to share with your partner, if and when you want to?
model.why: Involves the relationship on her terms

model.text: Maybe. I’ll think about it.

If your mood drops, if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, or if anyone starts to hurt you, please contact us straight away, or call 999 in an emergency. And if you notice unusual discharge, sores or bleeding, let me know. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
Self-swabs, a referral for the memories and for the sex side, the support details, and no examination unless I choose.
Exactly. I’ll see you again in a few weeks, with the swab results, just to see how you’re doing. You’re in charge of the pace.

social.t: Sexual difficulty strains relationships. Offer information she can share with her partner, on her terms.
Rape crisis services and SARCs support people after recent and past assaults, including emotional support without a police report.

legal.t: An adult decides whether to report a sexual offence to the police. Confidentiality can be broken only where there is a risk of serious harm to others, such as children (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain, offer a chaperone, get consent, and stop when asked. Trauma-informed practice means offering choice and control.
NICE PH50 (2014): ask about abuse in private; refer to specialist services if there is current abuse.
Offer to see the same clinician again so she does not have to repeat her story.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies for trauma-focused therapy (self-referral in England); psychosexual services via sexual health or gynaecology.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm — assess risk the same day
Current abuse or coercion — risk assessment and specialist referral
Postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, or deep pain with fever — assess promptly
Children in contact with the perpetrator — consider safeguarding
psychosocial: Impact on her relationship and self-image
ice: Idea: “It’s because of what happened — I’m broken”
Concern: it won’t improve; having to tell the story; examination

playbook.diagnosis: “The tightening sounds like your body protecting itself after a frightening experience. It’s a recognised response and it’s treatable. We’ll also make sure nothing physical is adding to the pain.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a flinch. Your body learned to guard itself, and it does it automatically. With the right help, it can learn that it’s safe again.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you feel broken. You aren’t. What’s happening is your body protecting you, and that can change.”
management.psychosocial: Let her choose the order of help, include her partner only if she wants, and keep the door open.
sharedPlan: Self-taken swabs now; examination only if needed and when she chooses
safetyNet: Low mood, self-harm thoughts or current abuse — contact straight away, 999 in an emergency
Review in a few weeks with results; same clinician if possible

pitfalls.intro: This station is about how you receive a disclosure. Candidates fail by asking too much, by pushing an examination, or by treating the pain as purely physical.

items.fail: Asking for details of the assault.
items.why: It is not needed for the plan and can retraumatise her. Examiners look for belief and restraint.
items.fix: “Thank you for telling me. You don’t need to say any more than you want to.”

items.fail: Saying an examination is needed today.
items.why: A pressured intimate examination after assault is harmful. GMC guidance requires consent and the right to stop.
items.fix: Say early that there is no examination today and that any future examination is her choice.

items.fail: Offering lubricant or dilators and nothing for the trauma.
items.why: It ignores the likely cause and the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Name the trauma link and offer trauma-focused and psychosexual help.

items.fail: Assuming it is all psychological and not considering infection or skin conditions.
items.why: Treatable physical causes can add to the pain.
items.fix: Ask about itch, discharge, bleeding and deep pain, and offer self-taken swabs.

items.fail: No question about current safety, mood or suicide risk.
items.why: NICE PH50 advises asking about abuse; low mood is common after trauma.
items.fix: Ask routinely and gently, and act on any risk.

items.fail: Telling her she should report to the police.
items.why: The decision is hers as an adult; pressure takes away control.
items.fix: “Reporting is entirely your choice, now or later.”

Superficial vs deep pain, infection or skin symptoms, PTSD symptoms, mood and suicide risk, current safety.
“I’m broken”, fear it won’t improve, fear of recounting the assault.
Trauma-related tightening, treatable; self-swabs; psychosexual and trauma-focused therapy; her choice on reporting.
Mood, self-harm, abuse, new physical symptoms. Teach-back and review.

wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: removes the fear of examination in the first minute; reframes the tightening as a protective response and gives hope; keeps physical causes in view with self-taken swabs; screens for PTSD symptoms; offers both trauma-focused and psychosexual help and lets her choose the order; is clear the police decision is hers; uses teach-back.

avoid.instead: "You don’t need to tell me any more than you want to."
avoid.why: Pressing for detail can retraumatise her and is not needed for the plan.

avoid.instead: "Reporting is entirely your choice, now or later, and there’s support either way."
avoid.why: For an adult, taking control away repeats the harm; the decision is hers.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; open question; let her disclose at her own pace; thanked her.
Explored the impact on her relationship, her stress and low mood, and her current safety.
Picked up “I’ve never really told anyone” and “can you fix it?” and responded to both.
Idea (it’s because of what happened; she is “broken”), concern (it won’t improve, having to recount it), expectation (to be fixed).
No examination today; offered self-taken swabs; examination later only if needed, with consent, a chaperone and control.
Vaginismus or trauma response vs infection, lichen sclerosus, dryness, endometriosis or pelvic infection; superficial vs deep pain.
Screened for PTSD symptoms, suicidal thoughts and current abuse.
Explained the likely trauma-related tightening in plain words, with physical causes still to exclude.
Trauma-focused therapy and psychosexual referral; sexual-assault support services; police reporting left to her; shared decision on priorities.
Addressed mood, the relationship and possible physical contributors.
Review in a few weeks with swab results; mood and safety safety-net; open door.

social.t: Sexual difficulty strains relationships. Offer information she can share with her partner, on her terms.
Rape crisis services and SARCs support people after recent and past assaults, including emotional support without a police report.

legal.t: An adult decides whether to report a sexual offence to the police. Confidentiality can be broken only where there is a risk of serious harm to others, such as children (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): explain, offer a chaperone, get consent, and stop when asked. Trauma-informed practice means offering choice and control.
NICE PH50 (2014): ask about abuse in private; refer to specialist services if there is current abuse.
Offer to see the same clinician again so she does not have to repeat her story.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies for trauma-focused therapy (self-referral in England); psychosexual services via sexual health or gynaecology.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts or self-harm — assess risk the same day
Current abuse or coercion — risk assessment and specialist referral
Postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, or deep pain with fever — assess promptly
Children in contact with the perpetrator — consider safeguarding

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The tightening sounds like your body protecting itself after a frightening experience. It’s a recognised response and it’s treatable. We’ll also make sure nothing physical is adding to the pain.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a flinch. Your body learned to guard itself, and it does it automatically. With the right help, it can learn that it’s safe again.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you feel broken. You aren’t. What’s happening is your body protecting you, and that can change.”
management.psychosocial: Let her choose the order of help, include her partner only if she wants, and keep the door open.

Review in a few weeks with results; same clinician if possible

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about how you receive a disclosure. Candidates fail by asking too much, by pushing an examination, or by treating the pain as purely physical.

items.fail: Asking for details of the assault.
items.why: It is not needed for the plan and can retraumatise her. Examiners look for belief and restraint.
items.fix: “Thank you for telling me. You don’t need to say any more than you want to.”

items.fail: Saying an examination is needed today.
items.why: A pressured intimate examination after assault is harmful. GMC guidance requires consent and the right to stop.
items.fix: Say early that there is no examination today and that any future examination is her choice.

items.fail: Offering lubricant or dilators and nothing for the trauma.
items.why: It ignores the likely cause and the hidden agenda.
items.fix: Name the trauma link and offer trauma-focused and psychosexual help.

items.fail: Assuming it is all psychological and not considering infection or skin conditions.
items.why: Treatable physical causes can add to the pain.
items.fix: Ask about itch, discharge, bleeding and deep pain, and offer self-taken swabs.

items.fail: No question about current safety, mood or suicide risk.
items.why: NICE PH50 advises asking about abuse; low mood is common after trauma.
items.fix: Ask routinely and gently, and act on any risk.

items.fail: Telling her she should report to the police.
items.why: The decision is hers as an adult; pressure takes away control.
items.fix: “Reporting is entirely your choice, now or later.”
